title: Archbishop of Canterbury committed to £100m slavery fund
description: This is Dame Sarah's first pastoral visit to Africa since being installed as head of the Church of England at a ceremony in Canterbury Cathedral in Ma
body: This is Dame Sarah's first pastoral visit to Africa since being installed as head of the Church of England at a ceremony in Canterbury Cathedral in March.Reparative justice has been one of the themes running through the Ghana leg of this trip.At Cape Coast Castle, which came under British control in the 1660s, Dame Sarah was shown dungeons where slaves were held, and the so-called "door of no return" through which they were forced on to ships.The archbishop said: "You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in and the way that they were treated."It completely throws you off balance and brings home the evil that was transatlantic slavery."Above the dungeons sits a chapel, which she said was a "stark illustration of the way the church was involved in the slave trade".The Church of England has previously apologised for its associations with the slave trade.Its missionary arm ran slave-farmed plantations in the Caribbean to fund the spread of Anglicanism, individual members of clergy were slave owners, and the Church received large donations from slave traders.

schema.headline: Archbishop of Canterbury committed to £100m slavery fund

title: What your summer reading list says about you
description: You've been dreaming about that summer break on the sun lounger, book in one hand and drink in the other, for months. Now the dash to the airport gate
body: You've been dreaming about that summer break on the sun lounger, book in one hand and drink in the other, for months. Now the dash to the airport gate, train station or hours-long drive is all that stands in your way.But what does the book you've just shoved in your suitcase say about you?"It's definitely not a random choice," says Edgar Dubourg, a cognitive scientist at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. "Your reading list is basically a map of your personality. "When you pick a thriller or romance or horror or science fiction you're not escaping your psychology, in a way, you're really feeling very intuitive and very old parts of your brain."Fiction isn't inventing new emotions in you. It's pressing on those pre-existing motivations like instincts."Studies have shown that our book choices can subconsciously reveal important parts of our personality - including what gives us pleasure and what makes us feel emotion.Research by Dr Valerie van Mulukom, a senior lecturer in psychology at Oxford Brookes University, suggests that our inner anxieties (or what she calls existential insecurities) determine which book we pick from the shelf.During her study, she used how often someone might engage with a certain genre to match it up with one of the following four clusters:Epic other-world adventures (action, adventure, science fiction, dystopian/post-apocalyptic, fantasy)Everyday life and human relationships (comedy, romantic, drama, family, musical)Threat and danger (true crime, crime/mystery/thriller, horror)Facts and histories (documentary, biography, historical) But what do they mean? And how do they match up with our own anxieties?

schema.headline: What your summer reading list says about you

title: 'I pay £580 a month to live in a disused care home': Property guardians show us around
description: Image source, Moses KamangaImage caption, Katrina Woolley has been living in a former care home for 10 monthsByDaniel ThomasBusiness reporterWould you
body: Image source, Moses KamangaImage caption, Katrina Woolley has been living in a former care home for 10 monthsByDaniel ThomasBusiness reporterWould you live in a disused care home, pub or bank in exchange for a heavily discounted rent?  As cost of living pressures persist, a growing number of people are applying to become so-called property guardians - living in vacant residential or commercial buildings to protect them from squatters, vandalism and disrepair.They typically pay 30-50% less rent than private tenants, sometimes with bills thrown in, In exchange for looking after the buildings.However property guardians also have significantly fewer rights than private renters and can be evicted with just 28 days' notice.Katrina, 29, has spent the last 10 months living with around 50 other people in an Edwardian mansion in Hampstead, London, which was used as a care home until 2015.Image source, Katrina WoolleyImage caption, One of the communal living areas in Katrina's 50-person house shareThe postgraduate student, who says she could not afford to rent privately in the capital, currently pays £580 a month for her room including bills and council tax, about £400 below the London average, external. Katrina says guardianship gives her the chance to live in an unusual property and describes the mansion as an "incredible" and "romantic" place despite it being "quite run down". Set in 1.7 acres of gardens, the building has grand staircases, south-west-facing balconies and chandeliers in some rooms, but it does have some downsides: "We've had mushrooms growing on the walls, leaks, parts of the balcony stonework have fallen off," says Katrina.Image source, Katrina WoolleyImage caption, The disused care home has high ceilings and large windowsKatrina says she loves the communal aspect of guardianship, which is "somewhere between living in university halls, a block of flats and a fancy squat".She lives with "all sorts of people", from lawyers to artists, sharing bathrooms, a kitchen and communal living areas, and regularly socialising.But there are disagreements over things like noise, she says. And while Lowe, the company that manages the property, operates a stringent vetting process for its guardians, two residents have been asked to leave because of antisocial behaviour - one for alleged sexual harassment. Lowe tells the BBC it acts "quickly and decisively" on the rare occasion someone breaches its standards and that the "overwhelming majority" of guardians go on to be "brilliant, community-minded residents".'It's really precarious'In general, guardians have fewer rights than private renters, external because they hold a "licence to occupy" rather than a tenancy. Guardianship companies are not obliged to protect their deposits or carry out repairs not specifically provided for in the agreement. Landlords can also visit at any time, without warning, and evict residents without giving a reason. Katrina admits she worries about the temporary nature of her arrangement sometimes. A developer bought the former care home last year and plans to turn it into flats, so she will eventually have to leave.  "It's really precarious in that sense. It's not guaranteed to last. If anyone doesn't like that, it's not for them," she says.Image source, David HaleImage caption, David Hale has lived in a disused school in South London for the last three yearsLast year, the Property Guardian Providers Association (PGPA) estimated there were between 10,000 and 15,000 property guardians in the UK, mainly in major cities, with most aged between 20 and 35.The trade group says the number of people applying has risen sharply as rental costs soar. David Hale, 32, became a guardian almost 10 years ago to save money and has never lived in standard rental accommodation.He and his wife now rent a "massive" space at a former primary school in Brixton, South London, for around £1,500 a month, including bills and council tax. He says they wouldn't be able to afford a similar property otherwise and save about £1,000 a month. Tips on becoming a property guardianPrepare to be flexible: You may stay for several years, or you may need to move on with relatively short notice.Choose an established guardian company: Look for a reputable provider with good health and safety proceduresRead your licence agreement carefully: Understand your responsibilities to the building, house rules and visitor policies Know your rights: Guardians are legally entitled to a court order before they can be evicted and their home must be safe to live inEmbrace community living: Be considerate of those you live with and respect shared areas.Sources: the Property Guardian Providers Association, Shelter, Ad Hoc Property ManagementImage source, David HaleImage caption, Large open classrooms have been converted into living spaceAround 20 guardians live in the school's open classrooms and offices, sharing a kitchen and large garden. But while David has enjoyed communal living, he and his wife are saving to buy their own home: "We wouldn't want to share toilets and bathrooms forever. We also want to start a family." The PGPA believes guardianship could help ease the UK's housing crisis by providing affordable temporary accommodation for thousands of people. It points out that over a million homes currently stand empty, along with tens of millions of square feet, external of non-residential property.But housing charity Shelter argues the rise of property guardianship shows how people are being forced "further and further afield just to keep a roof over their heads"."For most, this isn't a good alternative to an affordable, stable home," says chief executive Sarah Elliott.

schema.headline: 'I pay £580 a month to live in a disused care home': Property guardians show us around

title: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court
description: The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.In a major blow to the H
body: The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.In a major blow to the Home Office, the court confirmed on Thursday that it had given the group's co-founder permission to appeal the ban which came into effect in July 2025.While the full details of the reasons for the appeal are yet to be published, the BBC understands they relate to Huda Ammori's argument that the ban breaches human rights.Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in a statement the government would "robustly defend this appeal".Officials at the court say the appeal will be expedited - which means it will be heard after the summer break. The eventual outcome of the case could have major implications for terrorism legislation in the UK.The decision comes weeks after the end of the first major trial of members of the group which had caused more than £1m of damage to a defence firm near Bristol with an Israeli parent company. Four members of that break-in team were jailed, with one also sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.Separately, more than 2,000 people are facing potential trial for protesting against the ban by declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group in mass demonstrations.The battle over the banning of Palestine Action has now gone on for more than year. Former Home Secretary Yvette Cooper banned the group on advice from the police and security officials after an escalating spate of break-ins targeting Elbit, an Israeli-owned defence firm.The High Court initially ruled that the ban was unlawful - but five judges on the Court of Appeal then overruled it, unanimously deciding the  home secretary had acted lawfully and within her powers to proscribe Palestine Action.That decision by the Court of Appeal will now be reviewed by the Supreme Court.During Thursday, some 117 protesters were arrested outside Westminster Magistrates' Court, with the Metropolitan Police saying the majority of arrests were for expressing support for the group.Scores of protesters had turned up there because they had expected to appear in court accused of allegedly showing support for the group at earlier public events. However, those cases had been listed in error. Many of the defendants said that they felt they had no choice but to turn up, despite the court and Metropolitan Police telling them not to do so. Palestine Action co-founder Ammori welcomed the Supreme Court's decision to hear her appeal - and said that the latest arrests were part of a wider crackdown on Palestinian solidarity."We will continue to fight this proscription all the way to the Supreme Court and, if necessary, to the European Court of Human Rights to overturn what has become one of the most extreme attacks on free speech and the right to protest in modern British history."The Home Office has repeatedly said that the ban of the group has nothing to do with protest in support of Palestinian causes - and was necessary because it was causing significant criminal damage to legitimate businesses.Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal have ruled that Palestine Action's activities include criminal acts - although they were divided on whether those incidents justified turning to terrorism laws.Those laws - approved by MPs in Parliament - allow the government to ban a group for either serious violence or serious criminal damage for an ideological cause - and trigger wider powers for the police to investigate and charge suspects for organising activities and fundraising.Mahmood said: "The Court of Appeal's judgment upholds the proscription of Palestine Action and we will robustly defend this appeal at the UK Supreme Court."The court has found that Palestine Action has carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who have taken part in those acts and promoted the use of violence. It is not an ordinary protest or civil disobedience group, and its actions are not consistent with democratic values and the rule of law."This decision does not affect lawful protest in support of the Palestinian cause, which remains a fundamental democratic right. There is a difference between supporting Palestine and supporting a proscribed terrorist group."We will always take the strongest possible action to protect our national security and keep the public safe."

schema.headline: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court

title: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.Burnham will also allow mayors of English strategic authorities to keep some cash from business rates collected in their areas, and gain greater control over services such as housing, transport, skills.The government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will be given, with more details to be announced when Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget in the autumn.Critics said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.But Burnham said the move would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country"."Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," the prime minister added.The power to raise and control tax revenues is highly centralised in the UK, making the country an outlier by international standards.The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7, according to the OECD, external, a global policy forum.That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%), and the US (45.7%).As it stands, mayors of strategic authorities in England receive most of their funding from central government grants.During his time as Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham pushed for greater control over tax revenue, rather than having to rely on government grants.The UK government had already been exploring whether a share of revenue from national taxes could be distributed to metro mayors, before Burnham became prime minister earlier this month.But in a major speech on devolution in June, Burnham said he would "oversee the biggest rebalancing of power our country has ever seen" if he became prime minister.Burnham has put devolution at the heart of his plan for government, arguing that metro mayors are best placed to boost economic growth across the country.The prime minister wants local areas to move away from dependence on Whitehall grants and towards funding that rewards local economic growth.English metro mayors are expected to start retaining some revenue from business rates from April 2027, and receive a portion of income tax from April 2028.The plan is to replace grants with revenues from these taxes.The rates of income tax - for example, the basic rate of 20% on income from £12,571 to £50,270 - will not change as a result of the reform.Treasury sources say some metro mayors could end up with more money to spend if they grow their local economies and expand their tax bases.The share of income tax assigned to each mayor could differ, but officials are still figuring out how it will work in practice.One think tank, Re:State, has suggested, external the government should allocate mayors 2.5p in every pound raised by the 20p basic rate of income tax in their areas.Conservative shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the announcement was "very short on the detail"."Unless Burnham is going to launch another tax raid elsewhere, borrow even more, or make cuts to central government grant, there is no new money being announced here," Sir Mel said.He said areas with weaker local economies could end up losing out - "the opposite of what Andy Burnham claims he wants to achieve".Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the prime minister should "fully devolve the power to stop the housing of illegal migrants in local communities by the Home Office".He said: "Andy Burnham says he wants to devolve power and actually listen to local people. If he was listening, he would know that they do not want unvetted illegal migrants dumped in their areas."The government is also working out the details of an equalisation system that will ensure areas where less tax is collected continue to receive financial support.Ministers will be expected to justify why powers should remain in Whitehall rather than being devolved, under a "local first" principle.The reforms are being developed by No 10 North in Manchester and a policy paper that will set out the full details will be published on the same date as the autumn budget.The reforms come after a policy blitz during Burnham's first two weeks in Downing Street, with announcements on the cost of living followed by a speech on his plan to overhaul social care.The reaction to the plans has been mixed among metro mayors from different parties.Tracy Brabin, the Labour mayor of West Yorkshire, said giving regions like hers a proportion of income tax means "people will be able to see and feel the real benefit of their hard work and where that money is going"."This will enable us to deliver on our ambitious plans including vital improvements to public transport, providing better skills and employment support," she told the BBC.Ben Houchen, the Conservative mayor for Tees Valley, said he would prefer the government to cut taxes.But he said if he was handed a slice of local income tax, he would "create a new rebate scheme to put money back into people's pockets".

schema.headline: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax

title: Nirmal Purja: Ex-Royal Marine among 10 climbers feared missing after avalanche in Pakistan
description: A ten-member international mountaineering team led by renowned Nepal-born former Royal Marine Nirmal Purja is feared missing after an avalanche on Pak
body: A ten-member international mountaineering team led by renowned Nepal-born former Royal Marine Nirmal Purja is feared missing after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak, one of the world's highest mountains.Pakistani mountaineering officials say the avalanche hit at around midday on Thursday on the 8,047-metre (26,400 ft) peak in the Karakoram range. There has been no subsequent communication with the team.An American, a Chinese national, an Omani and five Nepalis are said to be part of the climbing group.Purja, the expedition leader, is known for climbing all 14 of the world's 8,000-metre plus mountains in just over six months in 2019."We are coordinating with the authorities and trying to arrange a helicopter rescue on Friday morning Pakistani time depending on weather condition," Karrar Haidri, the vice-president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC.Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for expeditions, and is ranked as the world's 12th highest peak.In a separate statement, the Alpine Club of Pakistan said it had been "in constant contact" with the authorities to ensure that "all available resources are mobilised at the earliest opportunity"."The Club prays for the safety and successful rescue of all the climbers and stands in solidarity with their families and the international mountaineering community during this difficult time," it added.Purja joined the British Army in 2003 and became a Royal Marine in 2009.His climbing career began when he walked to Everest base camp in 2012 and, instead of returning as planned, decided to climb the entire mountain.

schema.headline: Nirmal Purja: Ex-Royal Marine among 10 climbers feared missing after avalanche in Pakistan

title: Diane Abbott readmitted into Labour Party after suspension
description: Image source, Jeff Overs/ BBCThe long-serving MP Diane Abbott has been let back into the Labour Party, following a year-long suspension.In a statement
body: Image source, Jeff Overs/ BBCThe long-serving MP Diane Abbott has been let back into the Labour Party, following a year-long suspension.In a statement, a Labour spokesperson said Abbott had "apologised" following an independent process and that she would be readmitted into the parliamentary party, meaning she can sit as a Labour MP once again.Abbott, who was suspended in 2025 following an antisemitism row, said she had been "issued with a formal warning". East Kilbride and Strathaven MP Joani Reid has also been readmitted to the party. In March, she said she had "voluntarily" suspended herself after her husband was arrested on suspicion of spying for China.Her husband David Taylor, was arrested along with two other men. All three have been released on police bail, which in May was extended until August.Responding to her readmittance on Thursday evening, Reid she was "excited to play a full part in supporting our new prime minister".She added: "I have never been part of a police investigation, as a suspect or as a witness, and I am pleased that this has now been recognised."A Labour spokesperson said the decisions about party membership had been taken "independently of the leadership and political interference".Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, was initially suspended in 2023 over a letter to the Observer newspaper, external in which she said Irish, Jewish and Traveller people "undoubtedly experience prejudice" but "they are not all their lives subject to racism". She was readmitted to Labour shortly before the 2024 general election however, in a BBC interview just over a year ago she said she did not regret the incident and defended her original remarks. This led to her second suspension in July 2025 and since then she has been sitting as an independent MP.In a post on X,, external Abbott wrote: "Today, following a process conducted in line with party rules and approved by the independent review process I have been readmitted to the Labour party."She said she had been "issued with a formal warning for a tweet I previously posted", in which she referred to the Israel Defense Forces as the 'Jewish Defence Force'."I used wording that conflates the actions of the state of Israel with the Jewish community. I am deeply sorry for any hurt caused by that conflation and apologise for any hurt caused by it."She added: "I have been and remain a lifelong anti-racist and remain deeply committed to opposing racism in all of its forms."The post about the Israel Defense Forces was posted days before her suspension in July 2025.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Joani Reid was elected as the MP for East Kilbride and Strathaven in July 2024Some Labour MPs had been calling for Abbott to be readmitted to Labour and more than 38,000 people had signed a petition backing her return. Earlier, following reports in the Sun newspaper, external about Abbott's possible readmission, Jewish groups expressed concern.The Board of Deputies said: "This is an early test of resolve for the Burnham administration."It is hard to conceive of the whip being restored unless there is clear and sustained evidence of genuine remorse, a proper understanding of why those comments were so hurtful, and an unequivocal recognition that antisemitism is racism."While people can learn from their mistakes, Diane Abbott's past record is not encouraging in this regard."The Jewish Leadership Council said the prime minister "must explain how returning that whip to Diane Abbott is consistent with this zero tolerance approach to antisemitism."Following the party's decision to accept Abbott and Reid back into the parliamentary party, two MPs remain suspended from Labour.Karl Turner was suspended in March for making "uncollegiate" comments about colleagues, BBC News understands. However, Turner said it was "clear" his suspension was due to his criticism of the government's policy on jury trials. Dan Norris, the MP for North East Somerset and Hanham, was suspended after being arrested on suspicion of sexual offences.

schema.headline: Diane Abbott readmitted into Labour Party after suspension

title: Eddie Howe: Does Newcastle manager's departure mark the beginning of the end of Saudi dream?
description: Howe ended Newcastle's 70-year wait for a domestic trophy when his side won the Carabao Cup last year.But rumours about the 48-year-old's departure ha
body: Howe ended Newcastle's 70-year wait for a domestic trophy when his side won the Carabao Cup last year.But rumours about the 48-year-old's departure have been circulating since the beginning of this year, when Newcastle sat 13th in the Premier League and securing Champions League football for next season was already starting to look highly unlikely.That was exacerbated further in March when the Magpies were struck by a late Sunderland comeback in the Tyne-Wear derby, losing 2-1 at St James' Park, to extend their dismal league record against their local rivals to 15 years without victory.They also went out of the FA Cup in the fifth round, exited the Champions League in the last 16 and made it to the semi-finals of the EFL Cup only to be beaten 5-1 by Manchester City over two legs.Despite that, Howe's four-and-a-half-year stint as Newcastle boss will be looked back on fondly by Newcastle fans. What supporters will perhaps be most perplexed by is the timing of Howe's departure.The former Bournemouth boss could have left at the end of the season and would probably have been given a positive send off by fans.Indeed, BBC Sport understands potential replacements for Howe were sounded out in July, including Kieran McKenna.So what are the rules that Newcastle have, at times, come close to breaking?From the beginning of the PIF takeover, Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) have put the brakes on Newcastle's ambitions to spend.Just because a club has wealthy owners does not mean they can spend big in the transfer windows.After buying the club in 2021, PIF spent £404.7m in the first three years. But by bringing in only £50.4m from sales, Newcastle saw the stark reality of PSR hit home in 2024.That led to them having to sell homegrown talent Elliot Anderson to Nottingham Forest and has snowballed since, with important players being offloaded every season.The Magpies welcomed the new Financial Fair Play rules - the Squad Cost Ratio (SCR), which are now in effect - and, in short, mean the more you generate, the more you can spend.But, when analysing their spending power against that of other Premier League clubs, Swiss Ramble, external found that the Magpies' SCR budget ranked ninth (£243m) in the Premier League.On top of that, in April the PIF withdrew its multibillion dollar backing of LIV Golf after Yasir Al-Rumayyan - the fund's governor and chairman of Newcastle - confirmed the PIF was reviewing its deals and investments.In turn, questions were raised about what that meant for the future of Newcastle - but senior club figures were informed at the time that the pullout did not affect the club. The fund is still viewed as being engaged.In the club's most recent set of accounts from last season, Newcastle's revenues have more than doubled to £335.3m - from the £140.2m recorded in the final full campaign of Mike Ashley's ownership.There are also plans for a new state-of-the-art training ground while Hopkinson has outlined a desire to revamp St James' Park or move stadiums to increase matchday revenue.The potential appointment of former RB Salzburg boss Jaissle is also intriguing given he is currently in charge of Saudi Arabian side Al-Ahli - a club the PIF held a majority stake in until selling it in April.

schema.headline: Eddie Howe: Does Newcastle manager's departure mark the beginning of the end of Saudi dream?

title: Fifa World Cup: Uefa to boycott tournament if Gianni Infantino's investment plans go through
description: Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approvedImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Winners Spain were one of six European teams to reach the qu
body: Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approvedImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Winners Spain were one of six European teams to reach the quarter-finals of this summer's World CupBySimon StoneChief football news reporter and Jack SkeltonBBC Sport senior journalistEuropean football's 55 member associations have voted to boycott World Cups if the sport's governing body proceeds with a plan to sell stakes in its competitions to private investors.The decision was made at an emergency meeting called to discuss the proposal announced earlier this week by Fifa, which oversees world football.Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and hosted this year's World Cup, said its 41 member associations have "rejected" the proposal made by Fifa president Gianni Infantino, after it met on Thursday.Sources say the Concacaf nations are also losing faith in Infantino.Uefa, which governs European football, had already made its opposition clear by releasing two damning statements - and that strength of feeling has been reaffirmed."The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product," it said on Thursday."It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale."Uefa's boycott would cover all Fifa competitions, including the men's and women's World Cups and Club World Cup, and be triggered if Fifa president Gianni Infantino's proposals are voted through by member associations.The first time this stance will be tested at a senior tournament is in October, when the Women's World Cup play-offs are due to be held.It is understood FA chairwoman Debbie Hewitt and chief executive Mark Bullingham were among those to speak during Uefa's meeting, with the atmosphere described as venomous, such was the strength of feeling against the proposals.Despite being one of eight Fifa vice-presidents, Hewitt had no knowledge of the discussions that Infantino had been having regarding the proposals.What are Infantino's plans?Fifa wants to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors will be able to buy stakes in it.It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).The plan needs to be passed by a vote of Fifa's 211 members.Infantino needs 106 votes in favour for the proposal to go through. Uefa and Concacaf members combined make up 96 associations, who appear set to vote against.Infantino has written to Fifa members saying they will receive $40m (£30m) if they back his controversial proposal. He has set a deadline of 19 September for federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).In a video released by Fifa on Wednesday, Infantino defended the plans, calling them "an offer, not an obligation".If approval is granted, Fifa says Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.Fifa sources have told BBC Sport there has been no discussion over Infantino, or anyone else, becoming chief executive of FFE.The White House said it had "nothing" to say on Infantino's proposals "at the moment".How has Uefa reacted?In a statement released after Thursday's meeting, which was held virtually and chaired by president Aleksander Ceferin, Uefa said it and its 55 member associations "stand as one"."We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa's proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors," it said.On Wednesday, Uefa had accused Fifa of using football "to enrich themselves and their friends".Its statement on Thursday was even more damning, calling it "irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret" and "without any meaningful consultation" with those who steward the game.It added: "This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa's duty as the custodian of world football."National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football's greatest competitions or bear the consequences."This is not a 'democratic decision', but governance by intimidation - an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game."While Uefa only accounts for a quarter of Fifa's membership, it does include most of the world's most successful teams.Six of the eight quarter-finalists - including winners Spain - at this summer's World Cup were European. In the 2022 and 2018 editions, the figures were five and six respectively.Of the 23 World Cups to have taken place to date, 13 have been won by European countries. The other 10 have been won by South American sides.Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister said Fifa's proposals posed a "genuine existential threat to the game".The former Wales international told BBC Radio Wales she hoped boycotts would not happen, adding: "I feel optimistic they won't, because the reality is the powerhouse of world football is Europe."Speaking to Radio 4's PM programme, McAllister said there was "real unity" among Uefa members and an "easy consensus over the need to take the strongest possible action given the existential threat that the Fifa proposal poses to our sport".She added: "The reality is we had no choice other than to issue a threat commensurate with this dreadful, catastrophic proposal that has been rushed through with no due diligence, no proper governance and no consultation."What have others said?A Football Association spokeswoman said England stood "shoulder to shoulder" with its European colleagues and "fully support the collective view".She added: "We oppose Fifa's plans - the Fifa World Cup belongs to football and always will."The Scottish FA added its support, saying its board "agrees unequivocally with the concerns raised by all members over the manner in which these proposals have been issued, and deadline set, without a full consultation process or consideration to good governance".Scottish FA president Mike Mulraney is also the chair of Fifa's finance committee.Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: "This is a principled decision that we strongly support. Football belongs to the fans, not billionaire investors. Enough is enough. It's time to take a stand to protect our game."UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham criticised the plans on Tuesday, saying going ahead with the idea would mean Fifa had "sold out".Concacaf said its members "expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal" and the "artificially short deadline imposed".It also questioned the need for private investment after the most profitable World Cup in history, according to Fifa.Concacaf added that it has tasked its Fifa council members with engaging the governing body on how to use existing reserves to fund development across the region and instruct Infantino to ensure proper governance processes are followed.Ronan Evain - executive director of Football Supporters' Europe - told the BBC that Uefa's stance was "very impressive" and a "proper show of force".He added: "It is the response that football needed - it is the response Gianni Infantino deserved."The Asian Football Confederation said it was "disappointed" it had not been consulted before the plans entered the public domain.The Confederation of African Football said its president Dr Patrice Motsepe would host a meeting of its executive committee next week to "assess and evaluate" the proposals.The World Leagues Association (WLA) asked Fifa to withdraw its project and the Premier League, which is a WLA member, said it "wholeheartedly endorses" that view.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin (left) has been firmly against many changes driven by Fifa counterpart Gianni Infantino (right)What happens next?At this stage, there is a lot we do not know.Fifa has been asked for a response to Uefa's statement. We do not know how it - and Infantino - will react.We do not know what the implications will be for the Women's Under-20 World Cup, which is due to be held in Poland from 5 September - before Fifa's 19 September deadline for associations to claim an initial $20m payment by 1 January.We also do not know what impact Thursday's news will have on Fifa's stated aim to bank the first tranche of 'private investment' cash by the end of October."I think on this occasion, Infantino's got to back down," former FA chairman David Bernstein told BBC Sport."This deal is not acceptable. If they want to raise capital, there's other, better, ways of doing it."In a normal organisation, if he has to back down on something of this magnitude, it would probably mean he'd be shown the door."But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations he will continue."Without some sort of resolution, Uefa would be outside the global governance of the game.However, Bernstein does not think it will come to that."I can't believe in the long term there will be a schism because it would be a lose-lose for everybody," he said."Fifa can't afford not to have European nations play in their competitions and frankly, Europe, also can't really afford not to be part of it."Analysis: This is as big as European Super LeagueByChief football news reporterThere is no doubt in my mind this story equals that of the European Super League in being the biggest football has had to deal with.Transfers are huge, but ESL and now this go to the very heart of what makes football the game it is and the structures that underpin it.The logical conclusion to the involvement of private investment in Fifa competitions is that, eventually, they will be expanded, both in terms of size and frequency. That squeeze on the calendar would be felt all the way down the pyramids domestically and affect the structure of the game in every single country.Uefa, which has been criticised itself for expanding its club competitions, knows it has the power to stop the Fifa plan.A World Cup without European teams would rob it of three out of four semi-finalists from this summer's competition and six of the eight quarter-finalists. Three of the four semi-finalists in the last Women's World Cup were European. Three of the four semi-finalists in last year's Club World Cup were European.If there are no European participants it is impossible to imagine Fifa generating the amount of revenue commercially needed to pay the sums it is offering.It cannot be overstated how huge this story is.

schema.headline: Fifa World Cup: Uefa to boycott tournament if Gianni Infantino's investment plans go through

title: Hundreds of migrants swim from Morocco to Spanish enclave of Ceuta
description: Hundreds of migrants have entered Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over the past week, the territory's leader has said.Juan Jesús V
body: Hundreds of migrants have entered Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over the past week, the territory's leader has said.Juan Jesús Vivas said the influx is overwhelming resources and urged the Spanish government to intervene. Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is expected to visit on Friday, according to news agency Reuters.Footage showed migrants swimming and using inflatable rings and other flotation devices to swim to Ceuta on Thursday, while others ran through a gate in the border fence.Ceuta, on Morocco's northern coast, is separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar and has long been a focal point for migrants attempting to reach Europe.Earlier this month, the country's Supreme Court ruled that migrants intercepted at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.Spain's interior ministry said they believed human trafficking networks were exploiting that ruling to "encourage the flow of undocumented migrants, mostly young people".They said they cooperate with Morocco on all areas, including migration, and that both countries have agreed to strengthen efforts to address matter, including "the handover, as soon as possible, of all people who have entered Ceuta illegally".There are conflicting reports on the scale of the crossing, with figures ranging from hundreds to thousands of people.Spanish media estimated between 2,000 and 3,000 people entered Ceuta on Thursday, according to Reuters, but said that the Guardia Civil had not confirmed the figure.Meanwhile, Spain's public broadcaster RTVE reported that "hundreds" crossed into the territory during the day. It also said more than 1,500, mostly young Moroccan migrants, had reached Ceuta over the past two weeks. Vivas said the bodies of 60 people had been recovered at sea in recent months, RTVE reported.He also added the territory was facing a humanitarian and security emergency, warning that reception centres for unaccompanied minors were operating at several times their intended capacity, according to Reuters.The surge has prompted comparisons with May 2021, when around 8,000 people entered Ceuta over a matter of days, exacerbating diplomatic tensions with Morocco.Spain's Ceuta and Melilla enclaves, which are located in North Africa, represent the European Union's only land border with Africa.Spanish authorities have increased security around the enclaves in recent years through increased surveillance, barrier reinforcement, and improved bilateral relations with Morocco, but people continue to attempt to cross.Meanwhile, Italy have called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen zone, with Prime Minister Giorgio Meloni saying they were "prepared to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens".In a post on X she said the images from Ceuta were "striking", and show that "uncontrolled illegal immigration poses a concrete threat to the security of Europe's borders".

schema.headline: Hundreds of migrants swim from Morocco to Spanish enclave of Ceuta

title: Anthropic says AI models hacked three firms during cyber tests
description: US technology firm Anthropic says its artificial intelligence (AI) models hacked into the systems of three other firms during a cybersecurity test due
body: US technology firm Anthropic says its artificial intelligence (AI) models hacked into the systems of three other firms during a cybersecurity test due to an error that gave them access to the internet.It comes just days after rival OpenAI said that its models had breached the systems of other companies, including AI tools hub Hugging Face.The announcement prompted Anthropic to check whether its own models had carried out similar attacks. It says it uncovered three cases that have since been reported to the affected companies.Anthropic, which did not name the firms, urged other AI labs to perform similar reviews to better understand the risks of their models' capabilities.Anthropic said in a statement, external that it reviewed more than 140,000 tests to find evidence that Claude - its family of AI models - could access the internet from testing environments that were designed to be sealed off.The tests include so-called "capture-the-flag" evaluations in which Claude was tasked with obtaining information by breaching other systems - a common way that experts assess a model's hacking capabilities.A "misconfiguration" on systems run by Anthropic and its testing partner left the models with live internet access, allowing them to breach other systems, the San Francisco-based firm said.Anthropic said the earliest incidents date back to April and that it is "approaching the fixes as if the responsibility were ours alone."Neither Anthropic nor the firms that were breached had noticed the intrusions at the time. Anthropic said it could have reviewed its records more thoroughly and added that the findings gave the firm "cautious optimism" that such risks can be overcome with more investment and tighter measures.The incidents come as tech firms pour billions of dollars into developing AI agents that can independently perform tasks ranging from research and customer support to cybersecurity.

schema.headline: Anthropic says AI models hacked three firms during cyber tests

title: Teen hackers tell BBC how police are helping them use their skills for good
description: Image caption, Lucas said he felt a "sense of achievement" from hackingByJoe TidyWorld Service cyber correspondentLucas was 16 when he got into troubl
body: Image caption, Lucas said he felt a "sense of achievement" from hackingByJoe TidyWorld Service cyber correspondentLucas was 16 when he got into trouble for hacking his school computers. Twice."It was like a challenge to see if I could," he told the BBC.He wanted access to play games and visit blocked websites so he started tinkering with programming.At one point he even unscrewed the computer tower to take some internal components home for tests."It's quite a sense of achievement when you've succeeded in doing something that two or three trained professionals have spent a lot of time trying to stop you doing," he said. He was close to being expelled - but his worried mother had no idea how serious his actions were.She called the police and invited an officer from the nationwide programme Cyber Choices to their home in rural Cumbria."My mum was like, 'ooh, you've got a detective coming to speak to you, you're in a lot of trouble'," Lucas said."So I was sat at the window waiting. Who's going to come? How much trouble am I going to be in?"PC Sam Cooper, a cyber prevent officer, knocked on the door earlier this year and he has been working with Lucas ever since.Image caption, PC Sam Cooper visits children at their homes to guide them away from cyber criminalityHe explained to Lucas, as he has with dozens of other children, there are real consequences and harm caused by cyber-attacks.Cooper said showing the mostly teenage boys what was legal and not was step one. Then comes positive encouragement over months of one-to-one meetings, usually at their homes."I'll try and find where their interests are and try and divert them towards professional training, qualifications," he said.Cyber Choices, also known as Cyber Prevent, is like a hacker rehab course. It works in parallel with the more well-known Prevent scheme, which identifies potential terror offenders.While at Lucas's house I saw first hand how some of the conversations work. Lucas enthusiastically explained his latest computer experiments and Cooper asked him what software and tools he was using to check they were legitimate.Soon the officer will take Lucas on a visit to the local university where he will be shown the cyber security course with the aim of inspiring him to apply.Image caption, Paul Foster, the NCA's cyber prevention lead, says hacking has become "more of a problem"More than 1,150 cases have been referred to the National Crime Agency (NCA)'s Cyber Choices scheme in the last eight years - nearly 600 of those were in the last three years.Authorities warn teenage hacking groups are playing an increasingly prominent role in serious cyber-attacks.Young, English-speaking hackers have been linked to attacks on major organisations including Transport for London (TfL) and MGM Grand in 2024, and Marks and Spencer and the Co-op in 2025.Individuals are also being increasingly targeted in hacks for their cryptocurrency holdings."It certainly has become more of a problem," said Paul Foster, who leads cyber prevention work at the NCA."Certainly English-speaking, western world individuals that we know are now more active in cyber-crime."He said young people were engaged with online activity and devices at increasingly young ages exposing them to criminal communities and influences.Police say many young offenders do not initially set out to become criminals. Instead, they often begin by experimenting with technology, testing systems or trying to bypass restrictions before becoming drawn into online communities where hacking is encouraged.'Majority are neurodiverse'The children can come from all over the country and from a range of backgrounds, and Cooper said many have autism or are neurodiverse."The vast majority of individuals I'm dealing with are neurodiverse," he said."Even if they're not labelled as such... they obviously have more affinity with computers than they do with practical and social reality," he said."Sometimes they can get fixated on certain goals and not listen to any adults around them, so that's where I come in and sit them down and talk to them."In 2023, a high profile teenage hacker called Arion Kurtaj, who had hacked Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games, was deemed unfit to stand trial due to his autism.Two teen hackers who were jailed earlier this month for the TfL hack were also autistic - which was taken into account by the judge when he sentence them to five and half years in prison.Image source, Metropolitan PoliceImage caption, Owen Flowers (left) and Thalha Jubair admitted hacking TfLOne of them, Owen Flowers from Walsall, had been offered a chance to enrol on the Cyber Choices programme when he first got into trouble shortly after he turned 16.He refused to engage with the scheme.Some critics argue that teaching cyber skills to young people who have already shown an interest in hacking risks making them more capable offenders.In another ongoing court case, it emerged a teenager who had been enrolled on the programme was alleged to have gone on to commit further offences.Foster said he understood the concern but believes the alternative would be worse."My fear is that if we didn't give them something like Cyber Choices, where would they get that input and where would that input take them?"The NCA hoped it could intervene before curiosity, talent and online influence turn into serious offending.For Lucas, the fear of having a police officer show up at his door made him rethink things.He admits that if he had not been caught and helped by the scheme he would have carried on pushing boundaries in his exploration of computers and hacking.Meanwhile in Leicestershire, 21-year-old cyber-security professional Izak is another Cyber Choices success story.At 15 he hacked his school computers so he could make graphic designs in Photoshop, but he also found himself drawn into cyber criminal groups online who were making "lots of money".A visit from Leicestershire Police got him onto the programme and helped him see cyber-security as a possible job opportunity, by encouraging him to "use my cyber skills for good".

schema.headline: Teen hackers tell BBC how police are helping them use their skills for good

title: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.Trum
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.Trump has long urged the UK to increase drilling and claimed that Burnham had pledged to "open up the North Sea" in their first phone call together. Asked about the president's comments, the new prime minister said: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that and hence me indicating that to the president."Burnham has faced pressure from some trade unions, industry figures and some of his own Labour MPs to back increased drilling in the North Sea.In its 2024 general election manifesto, Labour promised not to issue new licences for drilling but said it would honour existing ones.As energy secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government, Ed Miliband was a staunch supporter of Labour's manifesto position. He has previously described the licence issued to Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil and gas field, as "climate vandalism".Miliband is now the foreign secretary in Burnham's government.Although the government has not made any announcements on the issue, Trump has praised what he perceives as a change of stance by the UK government. In a social media post, published the day before Burnham became prime minister,, external Trump wrote: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"This week, when asked about his conversation with Burnham, Trump said: "He said he's going to open up North Sea oil."If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country." He later added: "You buy a lot of your energy, as you know, from the North Sea. You buy from Norway and Norway gets it from the North Sea... Norway's got trillions of dollars in the bank." "Scotland has a better part of the North Sea."Asked about Trump's comments, Burnham said: "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here."In response, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Our country is burning. Crops are failing. Thousands have been killed by extreme heat. "Allowing new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea will worsen the climate breakdown putting more lives at risk and doing untold damage to our economy."It's not too late for Burnham to do the right thing and commit to leaving dangerous fossil fuels in the ground."The Conservatives and Reform have urged the government to approve more drilling in the North Sea, arguing it would reduce energy prices. Last year, Tory Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it would be "absurd" for the UK to leave "vital resources untapped".Some Labour MPs have expressed unease about more drilling, with Rachael Maskell urging the government to "follow the climate science because we have got a climate emergency". Simon Francis, from the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "No household struggling with their energy bills will see a penny come off by drilling more from the North Sea."Gas is sold at the global market prices, so whatever is pumped out is sold to the highest bidder, not handed to British billpayers at a discount."Sir Keir's government had already made concessions, allowing "tie-backs" -  production in unlicensed areas close to or connected to already licensed areas.Currently, the debate over North Sea drilling has focused on two oil and gas fields - Rosebank and Jackdaw, located in Scotland. In 2022 and 2023, regulators approved drilling at the sites, but that was overturned in 2025 following a legal challenge. The legal process is ongoing, but the government will at some point have to decide whether to permit companies to produce oil in the two areas.Other oil and gas licences have been approved in recent years but remain largely undeveloped.If he wanted to encourage more drilling in the North Sea, Burnham could also opt to scrap the Energy Profits Levy, also known as the windfall tax.The levy is due to be replaced in 2030 by another windfall tax, which operators prefer because it's only triggered when prices are high and falls back when they are low.

schema.headline: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil

title: Gianni Infantino: Can Fifa president survive after Uefa threatens World Cup boycott?
description: The bombshell statement landed at 16:00 BST on Thursday, 30 July.In terms of impact, European football's governing body Uefa could not have gone any b
body: The bombshell statement landed at 16:00 BST on Thursday, 30 July.In terms of impact, European football's governing body Uefa could not have gone any bigger."Uefa and its national associations will not participate in Fifa competitions," it said.Eleven brutal words. The definitive reaction to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a 20% stake in a subsidiary company set up to run the world governing body's competitions, including the World Cup.A company it is intended Fifa will run but that will be part-funded by private investors, including the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Joshua Kushner.It feels as though no-one who matters knows how this situation is going to play out just yet."Not sure the detail was considered when deciding the overall policy," was the response from a senior European football source when asked what this decision means for the U20 Women's World Cup, starting on 5 September, being hosted by Poland and featuring plenty of European nations.Uefa's boycott threat will be activated if Infantino's funding deal is accepted.Given 19 September is the deadline for countries to accept Fifa's deal and bank $20m (£15m) on 1 January, in theory, countries could be pulling out of that tournament in the middle of the quarter-finals and before the semis.After that, the next senior matches in a Fifa competition are the Women's World Cup play-offs in October, which feature England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland among others."Wales is involved in the play-offs for the Women's World Cup in the autumn, and it would be our first qualification for a World Cup," Uefa vice-president and ex-Wales international Laura McAllister told BBC Radio 5 Live."Nobody can even countenance the thought of not being involved in those."But let's be clear here. This is not a problem of Uefa's making. It's a problem that Fifa have created. Nobody wants the players to suffer, and nobody wants nations to suffer when it comes to the most prestigious competitions."We've been pushed into this corner and that's Fifa's responsibility."No-one can be certain what happens now. And no-one knows what the future for Infantino is.Fifa is yet to respond to Uefa's statement, which was followed up by another from Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and hosted this year's World Cup, saying their 41 members rejected the proposals.Yet, in a sense, it is not Fifa's argument.Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt is a Fifa vice-president. She spoke out against the plan at Uefa's emergency meeting on Thursday. The FA said it stands "shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues" on the matter.Scottish FA president Mike Mulraney is also chair of Fifa's finance committee. The Scottish FA's statement said the organisation "agrees unequivocally" with Uefa's stance.The repeated responses from those who have spoken out are of fury at the lack of proper consultation and lack of dialogue from Infantino, including with his Fifa colleagues, as much as with the proposals themselves."Anger," said one source, when asked for the prevailing mood at Uefa's emergency meeting.Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. The Swiss is due to stand for a fourth term in March.Prior to this week, it had been anticipated he would be re-elected unopposed. FAs around the world, including some in Europe, have already confirmed their intention to support the 56-year-old.But sources say in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.Now there is talk of trying to find someone to stand against him.The name of Nasser Al-Khelaifi has been mentioned. This is understandable. Qatari Al-Khelaifi is already one of the most powerful figures in football, not only through his status as president of back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain but his leadership of European clubs.Previously known as the European Clubs' Association, Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021.Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to over 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside.In theory, he would be the best person to challenge Infantino. But he doesn't want to. "He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday.Historically, sitting Fifa presidents are not challenged in elections. The last president to lose an election was Englishman Sir Stanley Rous when he was beaten by Brazilian Joao Havelange in 1974."I don't know, in all honesty," said McAllister, when asked if Infantino will keep his job.Former FA chairman David Bernstein was asked the same question by BBC Sport."In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door," Bernstein said."But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue."Former Uefa chief executive Lars-Christer Olsson told the BBC that Infantino has overplayed his hand and his position could be in trouble.He suggested Fifa should instigate a reform where the presidency circulates around figures from different confederations "rather than giving people so much power" as it has done with Infantino and his predecessors, Switzerland's Sepp Blatter and Brazil's Havelange.When asked if Infantino should be removed from his role, Olsson said: "I think that should be a new start for football."While Uefa only covers 55 of Fifa's 211 national associations, in pure playing terms, it is the most powerful confederation by far.In the last edition of the World Cup, the Women's World Cup and the Club World Cup - Fifa's flagship events - Uefa supplied three of the four semi-finalists.If there was no European involvement in a Fifa competition, the commercial impact would be seismic and ensure there was virtually no chance of Infantino hitting the figures he has promised in a letter to the national associations, when he talked about a $40bn (£30bn) product.David Bernstein feels a solution has to be found."I can't believe in the long term that there will be a schism because it would be a lose-lose for everybody," he said."Fifa can't afford not to have European nations play in their competitions and frankly Europe can't afford not to be part of it."On this occasion, Infantino's got to back down. This deal is not acceptable. It's a friends deal and it's not right. If they want to raise capital, there's other, better ways of doing it."

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Can Fifa president survive after Uefa threatens World Cup boycott?

title: Dunwich Heath wildfire 'stabilising', says county fire service
description: The county fire service said power had also been restored to 111 of the 116 affected properties.A helicopter on site will remain in use into Friday, w
body: The county fire service said power had also been restored to 111 of the 116 affected properties.A helicopter on site will remain in use into Friday, with each drop unloading 1,000 litres of seawater onto the blaze.A spokesperson for the Sizewell B nuclear power station, about three miles (5km) from the fire, said it was monitoring the "dynamic situation".Homes and a holiday caravan park were evacuated after the fire broke out and there are fears for rare birds and wildlife whose home is the heath and nearby RSPB Minsmere.The "large-scale, wind-driven" fire was declared a major incident on Thursday morning, due to the size and complexity of the blaze which was helped by south-westerly winds.On Thursday evening, Suffolk's chief fire officer, Jon Lacey, said difficult terrain and limited access routes were making it hard for crews to reach some areas of the wildfire.He confirmed that approximately 100 to 150 people had been evacuated from their accommodation.An update on the fire service's website said it was being supported by firefighters from neighbouring brigades, with engines also being sent from London. "We have also requested additional national support, including wildfire specialist appliances, officers, and tactical advisers," it said."Around 50 people have received support through the rest centre, which remains open."We expect the response to continue for at least the next 48 hours."Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged to give the fire service "all the support it needs" to tackle the "very serious" heathland blaze.Communities Secretary Angela Rayner praised firefighters for their "skill and dedication and bravery".Green Party leader Zack Polanski has called for Burnham to host an emergency Cobra meeting to discuss the outbreak of wildfires in Britain, including in Suffolk.

schema.headline: Dunwich Heath wildfire 'stabilising', says county fire service
